meta.title: Twice the Fruit, One Pan
meta.skill_frame: Process: see that doubling every amount does not double every step.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.73, 5.73 and 5.78 on the three parts (105, 102 and 109 words), 5.75 together. The load is a ratio: the amounts double, the pan's top does not, and the reader must work out which of the two decides the boil.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for process 4.3, band 4.3, sequence 2. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A jam kitchen doubling a batch in the same pan, where the surface that lets water escape does not double with the fruit.
source.avoided: No kitchen name, county, fruit variety, price, or jar count. No claim about how long a batch keeps.

session.difficulty_basis: One quantity on the list does not scale with the others, so a step that depends on the pan gets slower instead of staying the same.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: A jam kitchen cooks its fruit in wide, shallow pans that sit over a steady flame. The cook weighs the fruit, the sugar, and the lemon juice, and writes each weight on a sheet pinned above the stove. Nothing goes into the pan by eye, and the mixture boils until it reaches the set point. The cook tests for that point by dropping a spoonful onto a cold plate and tipping it. A shallow pan sets faster than a deep one, because water leaves through the top of the mixture. The top of a wide pan is the part that grows when the pan grows.
passage.part_2: One morning the order doubles. The cook doubles the fruit, the sugar, and the lemon, and pours the lot into the same pan. The pan is now twice as deep, and its top is the same width as it was before. Water leaves through that top, so the pan loses water at the same rate as it did with half the fruit. There is twice as much water to remove, and no second top to help it leave. The boil therefore runs much longer than twice the old time, and a long boil darkens the color and pushes the flavor toward caramel.
passage.part_3: The recipe is a list of amounts, and every amount on it doubles. The pan is not on the list, and the pan is what decides how long the boil runs. A cook who doubles the fruit and keeps one pan pays twice: in time at the stove, and in the color of the jam. The fix is a second pan or a wider one, so that the surface grows along with the fruit. What has to scale is the surface, not the depth. The sheet above the stove records the amounts and says nothing about the surface, so the cook has to supply that part of the plan.

items.prompt: How does the cook test whether the jam has reached the set point?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. A spoonful dropped on a cold plate.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the cook tests for the point by dropping a spoonful onto a cold plate and tipping it.
tutor_only.tell: The cook drops a spoonful on a cold plate and tips it.
help: The sentence about the set point names the test the cook uses.
It involves a cold plate and a spoonful of the mixture.
tutor_only.core_idea: By dropping a spoonful on a cold plate and tipping it.
accept_ideas: a spoonful on a cold plate
she drops a spoonful and tips the plate
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the cook watches the clock
if_they_say.ask: The passage gives a test with a plate. What does the cook do with it?

items.prompt: The cook doubles every amount and uses the same pan. Why does the boil take much longer than twice the old time?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The top stays the same width while the water doubles.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the pan's top is the same width as before, so water leaves at the same rate while twice as much has to go.
tutor_only.tell: The top of the pan is the same width. Twice the water leaves through the same surface.
help: The sentence about the pan's top says what stayed the same.
Water leaves through the top, and that top did not grow.
tutor_only.core_idea: Because the pan's top is the same width, so water leaves at the old rate while twice as much must go.
accept_ideas: the top did not widen, so the water leaves at the same rate
there is twice the water and the same surface
the pan is deeper but no wider
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the flame is too small for a big pan
if_they_say.ask: The passage points at the top of the pan, not the flame. What did not grow?

items.prompt: Why does a shallow pan set faster than a deep one?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Its top is wide for the amount of fruit in it.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says water leaves through the top of the mixture, and the top of a wide pan is the part that grows when the pan grows.
tutor_only.tell: Water leaves through the top. A shallow pan gives each part of the mixture more top.
help: The sentence about the shallow pan says where the water goes.
More surface for the same amount of fruit means faster setting.
tutor_only.core_idea: Its top is wide for the amount of fruit, so more water can leave at once.
accept_ideas: the surface is wide for the amount of fruit
more of the mixture touches the top
there is more surface for the water to leave from
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says a shallow pan gets hotter
if_they_say.ask: The passage is about water leaving, not heat. What does the wide top allow?

items.prompt: The cook says what has to scale is the surface, not the depth. Why?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The surface is what lets the water leave.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the pan decides how long the boil runs, and the fix is a wider pan so the surface grows with the fruit.
tutor_only.tell: The top is where water leaves. A deeper pan only adds water to remove.
help: The sentence about the fix names what has to grow.
A wider pan and a deeper pan hold the same fruit. Only one of them helps.
tutor_only.core_idea: Because the surface lets the water escape, so it must grow with the fruit.
accept_ideas: the top is what lets the water out
a deeper pan only adds water to remove
the width has to grow with the batch
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says a deeper pan holds more fruit
if_they_say.ask: Holding more is not the problem. Which part of the pan lets water leave?

items.prompt: A second batch doubles as before but uses a pan twice as wide. How does the boil compare with the old one?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The surface doubled with the fruit, so the boil stays close to the old time.
tutor_only.correct_reason: With twice the fruit and twice the width, the escaping surface doubles too, so the rate of loss keeps up with the water to remove.
tutor_only.tell: Twice the fruit and twice the width means the surface kept up. The boil stays near the old time.
help: The passage ties the boil to how fast water leaves through the top.
Both the fruit and the top doubled, so the two cancel.
tutor_only.core_idea: It runs about as long as the old one, because the surface grew with the fruit.
accept_ideas: it stays close to the old boil
much shorter than the doubled batch in one pan
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says it takes twice as long because there is twice the fruit
if_they_say.ask: In the first case the top stayed the same. What changed about the top here?
